claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Tungsten content provides the alloy with a high melting point.
Tungsten content provides the alloy with good thermal conductivity.
Tungsten content provides the alloy with low tritium retention.
High-entropy alloying of tungsten with refractory elements such as Ta, V, and Ti improves irradiation resistance relative to conventional tungsten.
High-entropy alloying with refractory elements mitigates helium bubble formation relative to conventional tungsten.
The proposed tungsten-dominated refractory HEA is single-phase and has a refined, coherently alloyed microstructure after processing such as spark plasma sintering.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K under high heat and particle fluxes involving D, T, helium ash, and neutrons.
High configurational entropy promotes a stable single-phase microstructure in the proposed tungsten-based alloy.
Coherent interfaces aid dislocation transmission and resist irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
A tungsten matrix gives the proposed alloy high-temperature resilience.
High-entropy effects suppress precipitation in the tungsten-based refractory alloy.
High-entropy alloying hinders helium bubble growth and thereby maintains mechanical integrity.
The proposed alloy reduces activation arising from neutron transmutation products.
The proposed tungsten-based refractory HEA will form fewer helium bubbles than conventional tungsten under simulated fusion conditions.
The proposed tungsten-based refractory HEA will retain less tritium than conventional tungsten.
The proposed tungsten-based refractory HEA will have better high-temperature mechanical performance than conventional tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a high melting temperature and low tritium retention, making it a leading plasma-facing-material candidate.
Pure tungsten suffers helium-induced bubbles, pits, holes, blistering, and associated surface damage under relevant exposure conditions.
The optimum composition and processing route for simultaneously achieving low activation and improved irradiation resistance have not been conclusively determined experimentally.
